I want to build something technically strong and genuinely useful at NASA Space Apps. I'm looking for teammates interested in programming, AI/ML, data analysis, astronomy, physics, or UI/UX. Beginners are welcome if they're curious, committed, and ready to contribute!
summary:
LunaSite is an open-source web app for comparing candidate landing sites near the Moon’s south pole between 2026 and 2030. I built it for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. You can put landing regions side by side, see where the Sun and Earth sit against a 360-degree terrain horizon, and check both solar power potential and direct-to-Earth communication windows.

Near the south pole, the Sun and Earth stay very low in the sky. Crater rims block them and cast shadows tens of kilometers long, which create cold traps and communication blackouts. Estimates that assume a flat horizon overestimate how much light a site gets. LunaSite fixes that by combining NASA elevation data with planetary ephemerides in a fast tool that needs no login.

Mission planners, teachers and the public can look at continuous illumination periods, find the best 7 to 30 day windows for a surface stay, and compare landing trade-offs in seconds.
details:
I built LunaSite to help evaluate landing sites at the Moon’s south pole. The Moon’s axis is tilted only 1.54° from the ecliptic, so the Sun and Earth stay close to the horizon. Crater ridges throw huge shadows, which means extreme cold at some sites and no line of sight to Earth at others.

To keep the app fast, I do the heavy math offline. A Python pipeline (SpiceyPy, NumPy and Astropy) feeds a web app that runs entirely in the browser (React 18, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS). The pipeline uses NASA NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440s ephemerides, in the topocentric MOON_ME frame) and NASA LRO LOLA elevation data (LDEM_75S_240M). It traces a 360° horizon out to 120 km from each site, corrects for the Moon’s curvature, and does this across 87,648 time steps from 2026 to 2030.

The web app loads in under a second. It works out five metrics: sunlit fraction, longest continuous darkness, direct-with-Earth line-of-sight fraction, longest communication outage, and power-plus-comms overlap. These feed a Mission Viability Score from 0 to 100, which you can rank by four presets: Rover, Static Lander, Crewed Stay and Education. A Best-Window Finder scans the timeline for the best 7, 14 or 30 day landing windows. You can scrub through a 360° horizon panorama that shows the Sun (0.53°) and Earth (1.90°) as discs against the terrain, switch between 2 m and 10 m mast heights, and read through a guided Learn section with a glossary.

Mission planners can use it for quick site trade-offs. Teachers can use it to show how polar lighting works, and anyone curious about the Moon can explore it. I think the mast-height comparison and the instant in-browser window search are the most creative parts.

It has limits. The elevation data is 240 m per pixel, so it smooths out small features like boulders. The time step is 30 minutes. Line of sight is purely geometric, with no radio multipath.

I built LunaSite with Super Intelligence (SI) assistance, using Google Antigravity (Gemini 2.5 Pro and Flash) for coding, testing and UI scaffolding, with my own review throughout. Details are in SI_USE.md.
